notes.meaning: David fled from the Philistine city of Gath and hid in the cave of Adullam, in the land of Judah. The name Adullam means "refuge," but God, not the cave, was David's real place of safety. His brothers and the rest of his family came to him, likely because they no longer felt safe at home from Saul's anger. Psalm 142 is titled as a prayer David prayed in the cave.

People in trouble, in debt, or bitter in spirit gathered to David, about 400 men. They were not the men David would have picked, yet he became their leader. He trained them into a disciplined band and never used them to attack Saul. Many readers see a picture of Jesus, the "Son of David," who welcomes broken and needy people and makes them his own.

David took his aged parents to the king of Moab for safety. Moab made sense because David's great-grandmother Ruth was from there, and Moab was Saul's enemy. His first care was to find his parents a quiet place, whatever happened to him, which is a lesson in honouring parents. His words "until I learn what God will do for me" show humble trust in God rather than in his own plans. His parents stayed there all the time David was on the run.

The prophet Gad, a messenger from God, told David to leave the stronghold and go back to Judah. This advice came from God, not just from Gad's own good sense. David was to show himself openly among his own tribe, as a man who knew he was innocent and trusted God. It also kept him from cutting himself off from his people and taught him to lean on the Lord alone.

Saul heard where David and his men were. He was holding court in the open air under a tamarisk tree at Gibeah, with his officials around him. Early kings carried a spear instead of a sceptre, but Saul's spear also hinted at the force and anger by which he now ruled.

Saul spoke to the men of his own tribe, Benjamin. He warned them that David, from the tribe of Judah, would never reward them with land and high posts as Saul had. Then he accused them all of a plot and claimed Jonathan had stirred David up to ambush him. None of this was true. Jealousy made Saul see enemies everywhere, and his self-pity was meant to push his men to act.

Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's officials, spoke up. He reported that the priest Ahimelech had asked God for guidance for David, given him food, and handed him Goliath's sword. His facts were true, but he left out that David had tricked the priest into thinking he was on the king's business. That half-truth is why Psalm 52, written about this event, calls Doeg's tongue deceitful.

Saul summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of Nob. They were what was left of the family of Eli, the priest whose house God had warned he would judge. All of them came, feeling no guilt. None tried to run to David, which shows they were not part of any plot.

Saul called the high priest only "son of Ahitub," not by his name or title. This was a deliberate insult and showed Saul had no respect for God's priests. Ahimelech calmly answered, "Here I am, my lord," as a man ready to hear the charge because he knew he had done nothing wrong.

Saul charged Ahimelech with joining David in a plot to overthrow him. He twisted simple kind acts, giving bread, a sword and prayer, into treason. It shows how innocent deeds can be made to look evil under a cruel ruler.

Ahimelech defended himself honestly. As far as he knew, David was Saul's most faithful servant, the king's son-in-law and a trusted officer. Asking God for David's guidance was nothing new, and he knew nothing of any quarrel. He did not even expose David's lie to him, though it would have helped his own case.

Saul ignored the truthful defence and sentenced Ahimelech and his whole family to death. He judged his own case, gave no reasons, and acted in a rage. The sentence fell even on family members against whom nothing had been said.

Saul ordered his guards to kill "the priests of the LORD," falsely claiming they knew David was fleeing. The guards refused. They feared God more than the king and would not kill innocent men who served God. The same Saul who would not destroy God's enemies, the Amalekites, now wanted to kill God's priests.

Saul turned to Doeg, and this foreigner killed 85 priests who wore the linen ephod, the simple linen garment of priests. Their holy clothing should have made anyone shrink from such a crime. Sadly, this also fulfilled God's long-ago warning against the family of Eli (1 Samuel 2:30-36). Saul was wicked in doing it, yet God was just in allowing it.

Doeg then destroyed the whole town of Nob: men, women, children, babies and animals. It is the worst act of Saul's life. He treated a made-up plot against himself as if it were treason against God. Meant to scare people from helping David, it turned good people against Saul instead.

One son of Ahimelech, Abiathar, escaped and fled to David with the news. God, in his care, kept his promise that one of Eli's family would be spared (1 Samuel 2:33). With his father dead, Abiathar was now high priest, and he brought the priestly garments with him. From now on both a prophet and a priest stood with David, God's chosen king.

David admitted he had seen Doeg at Nob and guessed he would tell Saul. He said, in effect, "I caused the deaths of your whole family." It deeply pains a good person to be the cause of harm to others. David's lie to Ahimelech was one reason this disaster happened.

David told Abiathar to stay with him and not be afraid. They had the same enemy, so David would guard him as he guarded himself. David spoke with confidence because he trusted God's promise to protect him and make him king. He could not undo the deaths, but he cared for the one who survived.
